column2: And Bríd Sheridan was fourteen miles up the road with the same hole in her accounts two years earlier, paying it out of her own savings so that nobody would ever have to use that word about her.
Eleven fault reports, one engineer, and a defect with a name, sitting in a document eight months before my mother stood up in a courtroom and said the word guilty.
The fault list went to every area manager in the country on the eighth of September 2016 and he opened it, because the read receipt is in her own mailbox on a thread he copied her into by accident.
Fast, loud, and it clears my mother's name in the only place my mother actually lives, which is a village of nine hundred and forty people.
I will ring her tonight and I will ring Bríd first, which is going to be the worst phone call of my life and I am not going to make somebody else make it.

The conviction of Máire Conneely was quashed in November 2029 on the grounds that the prosecution had failed to disclose material bearing directly on the reliability of the evidence — specifically fault report MER-2016-0114, defect OVERNIGHT, and the eleven duplicate reports filed against it before her trial.

On the twelfth, the shutter of the shop went up for the first time in nine years, because the man who bought the building put a table outside it and about two hundred people came, and Máire Conneely stood at the door of her own post office and shook hands until her arm hurt.

Aoife drove down on the Saturday morning and put four hundred and sixteen photographs, one fault list and one read receipt on her mother's kitchen table, and then sat there for two hours while Máire went through them in order without saying anything.

column2: I have read Tuesday's judgment and I am writing to you before you read about it anywhere else, because I think you will have questions and I would rather you put them to me than to a newspaper.
A woman stopped me at the church and said she was sorry and I could not tell whether she was sorry it happened or sorry I did it, and I did not ask, and I have thought about it every week since.
I counted the shopping twice today, on the table, in front of Peadar, and I did not know I was doing it until he went out of the room.

Nobody was at the counter of the area office so I put them through the letterbox in an envelope with the branch number on it, and I stood outside for a minute afterwards because I did not know what to do next.
I have said it about the trains and about the shopping and about the phone calls, but not about the second row, because to say thank you for it I would have to say what you were sitting through.
Before I ring you I want to ask you one thing and I would rather ask it in writing because I will not be able to ask it out loud.
Every year we hear from customers about a postmaster who has gone beyond what the job asks — who has walked a pension up a lane, who has known when something was wrong.

I said a word in a room in Galway that was not true because a man in a wig told me it would cost me less, and it has cost me every single day since, and I would like somebody to have heard me say that.
You are the straightest person I have ever met in my life and I have never once thought otherwise, not for a second, not in the room, not after.
It is that every one of those people said they were innocent, and kept saying it, for years, to anybody who would listen, and that is why there is a programme about them.
